newsitem.title: FINLAND: Better growth, jobs outlook in EMU than out-Finland.
newsitem.headline: Better growth, jobs outlook in EMU than out-Finland.

text.p: The Finnish finance ministry said in a report on Thursday the prospects for economic growth and a favourable employment trend would be better inside the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) than outside it.

"Economic and Monetary Union will not solve Finland's main topical problems. It will, however, provide better conditions for favourable growth and employment trends than remaining outside the Euro-area," the ministry said.
"EMU will enhance the pre-requisites for an economic policy that supports growth and employment," it said.
The finance ministry said fiscal and monetary policy might have to be "unnecessarily tight" to earn economic policy credibility outside the third phase of EMU. This would lead to slower growth.
Living with EMU would require adjustments in many sectors, it said.
Addressing the labour market organisations, the finance ministry said the collective wage bargaining system would not be forced to change if Finland entered EMU.
"But the system must be able to adjust to conditions of permanently low inflation, and, if necessary, accept lower nominal wages required by economic realities," it said.
In EMU, conditions for moderate wage development would be better, the finance ministry said.
"(But)...under some circumstances, it could be desirable from the point of view of employment that the price of labour could flex downwards," it said.
Such a circumstance could be that a strong and long-term economic disturbance hit the Finnish economy while the effects of it on other EMU-member countries remained slight, the report said.
In that scenario, the continuation of corporate activities "could require a fall in labour costs," it said.
In Finland, the forest industry would be especially vulnerable to external shocks not felt as strongly in other countries, the finance ministry noted.

"In conditions of the single currency, monetary policy and the exchange rate of the Euro would smooth out the fluctuations in this for Finland's central sector only to an extent corresponding to average cyclical changes," it said.
"Companies, and in the next stage the labour force and raw material suppliers would have to bear the brunt of the effects of the shock," it added.

The finance ministry said the third phase of EMU would not change the already existing objectives of Finland's economic policy, which include sustained growth, low inflation, turning state indebtedness into decline and improved employment.
Opting out of EMU would not change the course of economic policy.

"States remaining outside the Euro-area must aim at a stable economy and sustained growth with the same kind of economic policy as the Euro-area countries, but in less stable conditions and probably at a higher cost," it said.
On the whole, the third phase of EMU was a project of such magnitude that it was impossible to draw unambigious conclusions of its effects, the finance ministry said.

The report was compiled by civil servant level economists and experts at the ministry's economics department, and their conclusions have not been endorsed by the government and so do not amount to official policy, a ministry spokeswoman said.
--Peter Starck, Helsinki Newsroom +358 - 0 - 680 50 245
